newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Gazprom seeks UES stake, UES says unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Gazprom seeks UES stake, UES says unlikely.

text.p: Russia's mighty gas monopoly Gazprom said on Thursday it was seeking a one-quarter stake in Russia's biggest company, national power group UES.

But UES, whose regional subsidiaries owe Gazprom billions of dollars, said the Russian competition authorities were unlikely to allow an acquisition to go through, although share analysts said it could be good for both firms.

Gazprom spokesman Anatoly Kotov told Reuters that RAO Gazprom intended to acquire 25 percent plus one share in Unified Energy System (UES). This would be enough to ensure it seats on the board of UES and prevent changes to UES's charter.
But a senior UES official said that the Anti-Monopoly Committee was unlikely to approve such a bold acquisition.

"Firstly, the anti-monopoly committee will not allow this, or at least it would be declared invalid. Secondly, if it wants to buy shares on the open market, it would be too expensive," said Alexander Lopatin, UES director of asset management.

Gazprom is the world's biggest natural gas company, one of Russia's richest corporations and immensely influential in Russia -- Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin headed Gazprom when it was still a ministry.
But RAO Yedinaya Energeticheskaya Sistema Rossii (UES) is also a force to be reckoned with. It is by far Russia's biggest corporate employer and its biggest company by sales in 1995.
UES operates Russia's national power grid, and accounts for four-fifths of its generating capacity, mainly through majority stakes in most of Russia's "energo" regional power companies.
These subsidiaries owe Gazprom about 20 trillion roubles ($3.5 billion), Lopatin said.
Giving Gazprom a stake in the management of UES would help solve the debt problem and improve UES generally, analysts said.
However, in the short term, UES shareholders could suffer.

Both Gazprom and UES are viewed by investors as monolithic, unresponsive structures more like the Soviet ministries they once were than competitive corporations. The Russian government says it wants to restructure both of them.
But analysts noted Gazprom has already issued securities on foreign markets, while they see UES as unfriendly to investors and opposed to foreign investment.
An acquisition would most likely involve Gazprom converting UES debts into equity, said Alexander Kazbegi, Russian utilities analyst at investment bank Salomon Brothers in London.
"That means Unified has to issue new shares and dilute existing shareholders... That would be a very bad thing for the other shareholders, but it's quite possible," he said.
"The cash position of Unified doesn't allow them to do anything else."
UES ended unchanged at $0.2315 on the Russian Trading System, Russia's electronic over-the-counter market.
But Gazprom jumped to $0.630 from Wednesday's $0.571.

Dealers said the Gazprom share price rise was probably due to comments by Gazprom Chairman Rem Vyakhirev in the Wall Street Journal Europe, saying Gazprom may be opening up to foreign investment in its domestic shares.
Gazprom strictly separates shares for domestic and foreign investors, and in its charter has set aside nine percent of its capital for non-resident investors.
Only one percent of this has been issued, in the form of American Depositary Shares (ADSs), which trade at a massive premium to the domestic shares.
The ADSs, equivalent to 10 underlying shares, fell in London to $17.825 from $19.425 on Wednesday as investors decided they could after all buy the domestic shares.
In practice, non-residents attracted by the price difference can already buy domestic shares through local front companies. Gazprom seems to have tacitly accepted this in the past.
A senior Gazprom official said Vyakhirev's remarks had not changed the company's restrictions on trade in its shares.
Non-residents could buy local shares but their ownership rights were still governed by the charter, said Eduard Ivanov, head of the securities department.
Gazprom had bitterly opposed a widely publicised plan by a unit of Regent Pacific Group to set up a foreign-based fund investing in domestic Gazprom shares through a local subsidiary.
Regent dropped the plan this week.
But today's surge in domestic Gazprom shares would have given it a useful opportunity to unload its shares now the deal has fallen through, dealers said.
